description: A group of passionate students dedicated to exploring Artifical Intelligence, Machine Learning , Data Science , Scientific Research and Creativity with different skillsets and passions
summary: The ‘Ascend to Ares’ prototype is a web based project which has been constructed to bring together images, points of interest and initial route comparisons from our Martian planet. This project answers the challenge from the ‘Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map’. It shows how we can utilise the data collected from missions to Mars and present it in a way that allows for exploration. This project illustrates how we can create useful exploration planning tools from the information available. By bringing together images, geological information and route planning, this project shows how complicated information can be made into a useful tool for exploration. It also shows how using observation and mapping tools can help make decisions based on information. This will help to create a more efficient and research driven exploration of Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works
Ascend To Ares is a web-based planning tool for comparing science exploration routes near Jezero Crater, Mars. A user starts on an interactive 3D Mars globe, then opens a Map Explorer built on USGS/NASA CTX orbital imagery and an elevation view. Toggleable layers show slope watch, geology regions, science targets, and terrain watch points. The user picks a start point and a science destination, and the app compares two routes using Dijkstra’s shortest-path algorithm on a graph of waypoints and targets. Route A is the direct route, with a light terrain penalty. Route B is the terrain-aware route. Edge weights use Mars-surface distance ( including Mars radius ) multiplied by a terrain factor built from slope, roughness, and obstacle values. Each route shows distance, moving time at an adjustable walking speed, a difficulty score, and a plain-language explanation of the trade-off. Both routes can be viewed in 2D or on a 3D terrain view, and an EVA time-budget tool checks whether a round trip fits in a chosen outing length with a 25% reserve. Science Guide links four targets to the questions they help answer. Environment Archive explains Perseverance’s MEDA measurements and a Curiosity radiation benchmark. Data Sources page links to the original records.

Benefits and intended impact
Planners can compare candidate walking routes early, before detailed analysis. They see that the shortest path is not always the best one, because terrain and science value matter too. Teachers, students and space fans get a hands-on way to see how orbital imagery, geology, mission science and route maths connect. The aim is to make planning a Mars surface walk clear, visual, accessible, and easy to understand, aimed at students, planners/researchers, teachers, and space enthusiasts, and for astronauts in the future. For future processes, we hope to compute slope and roughness from the CTX or HiRISE DEM and validate hazards against mapped features.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript , with no third-party dependencies and no build step.
  • ChatGPT is used for refining some parts of the code and basic debugging, as well as accelerating the process of coding and the overall project, such as ideas and help in brainstorming.
  • Three.js for the 3D globe and 3D terrain view.
  • A Node.js development server, with a Python fallback server, and a project check script.
  • Data and imagery from USGS Astrogeology (CTX orthomosaic, CTX DEM, geologic map of Jezero), NASA PDS (Perseverance MEDA), the Curiosity RAD summary, and NASA/JPL-Caltech Perseverance images.

Creativity
Instead of a plain map viewer, we combine real orbital data, mission-planning logic, and science storytelling in one interface. Routing is built around a science question (“choose a reason to go”), not just getting from A to B. Showing a shorter route beside a terrain-aware route makes the trade-off visible. The 3D terrain is estimated from the colours of the elevation image, so a lightweight site can show relief without multi-gigabyte raster files.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: the slope, roughness, and obstacle values in the route graph are demonstration values, not calculated from the DEM. The 3D heights are a visualization, not measured elevation. Environmental data are historical records, and the radiation figure comes from Curiosity at Gale Crater, not Jezero. Travel time ignores rest, sampling, suit limits, and emergency margin. All of this is labelled in the app, and the project is described as an educational prototype, not for mission use.
  • Accuracy: distances use Mars’s radius, and coordinates are planetocentric, east-positive.
  • Accessibility and usability: skip link, ARIA labels, a dark colour scheme, a “Start here” hint, and a mobile menu ensuring a smooth UI/UX experience
  • Portability: it runs locally with one command and needs no installs
